query: Which method can be used for high-temperature oxidation behaviour and phase stability, and why?

generation.hypothesis: In situ high‐temperature X‐ray diffraction (HT‐XRD) can be used to monitor the oxidation behaviour and phase stability of high-entropy alloys by detecting the formation of stable oxide phases (such as spinel) at elevated temperatures.
generation.material_initial_state: A high-entropy alloy produced by powder metallurgy and spark plasma sintering, exhibiting a dense multiphase microstructure (e.g., AlCoCrFeNiTi0.5 with bcc phases and minor σ-phase).
generation.intervention: Expose the alloy to an oxidizing atmosphere at temperatures in the range of 800–900 °C.
generation.conditions: High-temperature oxidation under ambient air with controlled heating rates, ensuring the test temperature remains within the 800–900 °C range.
generation.structural_mediator: Formation of a protective oxide layer, particularly a spinel phase, on the surface of the alloy.
generation.mechanism: At elevated temperatures, the alloy surface undergoes oxidation. HT-XRD is expected to capture the formation of new diffraction peaks corresponding to oxide phases (e.g., the spinel structure), indicating a transformation that confers oxidation resistance and enhances phase stability.
generation.predicted_outcome: HT-XRD will reveal the emergence of characteristic diffraction peaks for a spinel phase at high temperatures, demonstrating oxide layer formation and an increase in phase stability compared to the baseline (unoxidized state).
generation.baseline: The initial crystallographic profile of the alloy obtained at room temperature prior to oxidation exposure.
generation.boundary: This method is effective when the oxide phases are crystalline and detectable by XRD; it may be limited in cases where oxides are amorphous or present in quantities below the detection limit.
generation.uncertainty: The precise temperature at which the oxide phase forms and the proportion of the oxide phase may vary with specific alloy compositions and processing conditions.

falsification_experiment.design: Perform an in situ HT-XRD experiment on samples of the alloy while gradually heating from 700 to 950 °C in an oxidizing atmosphere. Record diffraction patterns at regular temperature intervals to monitor phase evolution.
measurements: XRD diffraction peak positions and intensities
Identification of oxide phase peaks (e.g., spinel)
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the HT-XRD does not show new diffraction peaks attributable to a stable oxide (such as spinel) in the expected temperature range, or if the appearance of these peaks does not coincide with an improvement in phase stability, then the hypothesis that HT-XRD is a valid method for assessing high-temperature oxidation behaviour and phase stability is falsified.
